description: The bar chart illustrates performance comparisons across various large language models (LLMs) on two benchmark datasets—MATH-500 and AIME24—grouped by model size and method, as part of a study rethinking compute-optimal test-time scaling. On the left, the MATH-500 results are divided into three subplots: (a) 3B–405B models using CoT and TTS; (b) 1.5B–unk models using o1-mini, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-1.5B, and o1-preview; and (c) 671B–unk models using DeepSeek-R1, GPT-4o, and o1. The y-axis represents accuracy percentage (65–100), with each bar labeled with its exact score. In (a), Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct (78.2) outperforms GPT-4o (74.6) and Llama-3.1-405B-Instruct (71.4). In (b), DeepSeek-R1-Distill-1.5B (91.6) leads, followed by o1-mini (90.0) and o1-preview (85.5). In (c), DeepSeek-R1 (97.3) and GPT-4o (95.2) are nearly tied, with o1 (94.8) slightly behind. On the right, AIME24 results are shown in three subplots: (d) 3B–unk models (Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct: 30.0, Llama-3.1-405B-Instruct: 23.3, GPT-4o: 9.3); (e) unk–1.5B–unk models (o1-mini: 63.6, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-1.5B: 63.3, o1-preview: 44.6); and (f) 7B–671B–unk models (DeepSeek-R1: 83.3, GPT-4o: 79.8, o1: 79.2). The y-axis here ranges from 0 to 90. Notably, smaller models like DeepSeek-R1-Distill-1.5B and o1-mini achieve competitive or superior scores to much larger models such as 405B and 671B variants, supporting the paper’s thesis that smaller, well-optimized models can surpass larger ones under test-time scaling. Each bar is color- and pattern-coded according to the legend, with model names and sizes labeled beneath each group.
